clips.title: Why Large Language Models Hallucinate
clips.why: The story's wrong answer has a name: a hallucination, a fluent answer that is not true. This part shows the kinds and some clear examples.
look: The kinds of hallucination: answers that contradict the facts, and answers that contradict themselves.
How confident and well written the wrong answers sound.
Ask yourself which kind the bot's made-up page path is.
clips.after: A made-up source is the most dangerous kind for the brain bot, because it makes a wrong answer look checked; that is why our code, not the model, decides which sources stand.

clips.title: RAG - but with Verified Citations!
clips.why: A short opening that states the problem of this lesson in general: an answer with citations is only useful if someone checks that the citations are real.
look: Why citations from a model need their own check.
The plan of the video: verify each citation against the source text.
Compare his check with ours, which asks git whether the cited file exists at the cited commit.
clips.after: Our first check is simpler and stricter about existence: a citation is rnd-kb/<path>@<sha>, and git either has that file at that commit or it does not.

clips.title: OpenAI Structured Output - All You Need to Know
clips.why: A clear explanation of structured output: you give the model a JSON schema and get back data your code can use.
look: What changes when the model must answer in a fixed JSON shape instead of free text.
The schema as a contract between the model and your code.
He uses OpenAI's API; Claude's Agent SDK takes the same kind of JSON schema as output_format.
clips.after: Our ANSWER schema has three fields, answer, citations and unverified, so the citations arrive as a list our code can check one by one.

clips.title: LLM Chronicles #6.6: Hallucination Detection and Evaluation for RAG systems (RAGAS, Lynx)
clips.why: The next problem after a real source: is the answer actually supported by it? This part names that idea, faithfulness or groundedness, and how it is measured.
look: Faithfulness: every claim in the answer can be found in the retrieved text.
Why a real source does not prove a faithful answer.
The metrics that score it, which are close to what our nightly BRAIN-QA judge does.
clips.after: For hard questions our bot adds a checker that re-reads each cited source and moves claims it cannot confirm into unverified, which is a faithfulness check done before the reply is posted.

practice.q: The model returns two citations. rnd-kb/engineering/code-run-path.md@30b0087 exists; rnd-kb/engineering/ci-map.md@abc1234 names a commit the mirror does not have. What does keep_resolvable return?

options.text: "I don't know", because one of the sources is wrong.
options.why: The answer is replaced only when no source is left. One real source survives here.

options.text: The answer with only the code-run-path.md source.
options.why: Each citation is checked on its own. The one git cannot find is dropped, and the rest of the result is kept.

options.text: The answer with both sources, because ci-map.md exists at the newest commit.
options.why: The check uses the commit named in the citation. abc1234 is not in the mirror, so that citation does not resolve.

practice.q: Finish the git command that answers only with its exit code: does this file exist at this commit?
practice.hint: A two-letter flag: e for exists.
practice.why: cat-file -e prints nothing and exits with 0 when the object exists, so the bot can test a citation without reading the file.

practice.q: Where does the check for patient-like data in the question run?

options.text: In the handler, before any model call.
options.why: A question that fails never reaches a prompt, costs nothing, and gets one fixed sentence back.

options.text: In the system prompt, which tells the model to refuse such questions.
options.why: By then the text has already been sent to the model. A wall that depends on the model can be argued with.

options.text: In redact(), after the model answers.
options.why: redact() cleans the reply. The question itself would already have gone into the prompt.

practice.q: Someone mentions @Rhino Brain in an allowed channel. Put what happens in order.
items: The handler checks the channel ID and scans the question for blocked words
Our code starts one Agent SDK session with read-only tools over the mirrors
The session returns JSON with answer, citations and unverified
keep_resolvable drops every citation git cannot find at its commit
Our code redacts the reply and posts it in the thread
practice.why: The cheap walls come first, the model works in the middle, and our code checks and posts at the end. The model never touches Slack.

practice.q: Why does the session get no Slack tool, even though its answer ends up in Slack?

options.why: Cost is not the reason. The reason is what a tool would let a fooled model do.

options.text: So that only our code posts, after the citation check and redact, and a page or question that tries to steer the model has nothing to post with.
options.why: If the model could post, every wall after the model call could be skipped. Without the tool, the model can only propose.

options.text: Bolt for Python cannot share its client with the Agent SDK.
options.why: It could be wired up. We choose not to, on purpose.

practice.q: Why is the bot written in Python when the rest of the agent platform is TypeScript?

options.text: It imports kb_tools in its own process, so it ranks pages and redacts exactly like the kb command and BRAIN-QA.
options.why: One shared package means the nightly test measures the same search and redaction that answer people.
Bolt exists for TypeScript too; Nova's Slack app uses it.

options.text: Structured output only works in the Python SDK.
options.why: Both Agent SDKs support structured output.
